mainTopic: Two rulings of רבי יוחנן: a גוי's share in an animal makes it exempt from בכורה even if that share is only a מום קל, and a mixed-looking firstborn (a goat-like lamb) counts as having a מום קבוע. The גמרא accepts the first ruling and asks what new point the second one teaches.
overview: This amud opens with two rulings of רבי יוחנן. First, a גוי's share in an animal cancels its בכורה even if removing that share would cause only a מום קל. Second, a firstborn that looks like a different species but has some of its mother's features has a מום קבוע and may be slaughtered. The גמרא accepts that the first ruling sides with רב הונא, but asks what the second one adds, since משניות already count a pig-like mouth and uneven eyes as blemishes. It answers that an eye as big as a calf's is a מום because the animal is a שרוע. It tries to support this from the person-only blemishes of a כהן, but rejects that proof: one big eye and one small eye could also be a plain שינוי, since health or weakness would affect both eyes equally. The גמרא then turns to partnership with a גוי. רבא tells a convert that nobody follows רבי יהודה, who says such a partnership is obligated in בכורה. רב מרי בר רחל sold the ears of his firstborns to a גוי, and his flock died. The גמרא gives two reasons: he removed even the כהן's holiness, which goes further than blemishing a fetus; or others might copy him without a proper sale. A new משנה then teaches that כהנים and לוים are exempt from פטר חמור, by a קל וחומר from the מדבר.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן: even a slight blemish is enough
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן rules that if a גוי's share in an animal would cause even a מום קל when removed, the animal is still exempt from בכורה.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what רבי יוחנן said: even if the part owned by the גוי would leave only a slight blemish, the animal is still not a בכור.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings רבי יוחנן's ruling about a firstborn animal partly owned by a גוי. Even a small share, one whose removal would cause only a minor blemish, is enough to remove the בכורה status.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier the גמרא discussed how big the גוי's share must be to cancel בכורה. רב הונא said even an ear is enough. רב חסדא and רבא said the share must be big enough that removing it would make the animal a נבלה or טריפה. רבי יוחנן sets the smallest possible bar: even a share that would only cause a מום קל counts.

keyTerms.meaning: The firstborn status and its holiness

phrases.english: This is what Rabbi Yoḥanan said:
Even a slight blemish.
phrases.notes: Even if the part the gentile owns would cause only a minor blemish when removed, the animal is exempt from firstborn status.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the earlier discussion of a גוי's partnership in a firstborn animal.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A גוי's share in an animal cancels its בכורה status even if removing that share would cause only a מום קל.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן on a lamb that looks like a goat
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן comments on a משנה: a lamb that looks like a goat but has some of its mother's features is a בכור, yet it counts as having a מום קבוע and may be slaughtered.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה teaches that a ewe that gave birth to a goat-like animal, or a goat that gave birth to a lamb-like animal, is exempt from בכורה. If the baby has some of its mother's features, it is obligated. רבי יוחנן adds that such an animal has a permanent blemish, so it may be slaughtered because of it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second statement of רבי יוחנן, this time on a משנה about a mixed-looking firstborn. He says such a firstborn counts as permanently blemished.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה rules that a baby that looks fully like a different species is not a בכור. If it shares some features with its mother, it is a בכור. רבי יוחנן adds that it is still not fit for the מזבח. Its odd look is a מום קבוע, so a כהן may slaughter and eat it outside the מקדש.

keyTerms.meaning: And regarding that which we learned in a משנה
To slaughter it because of that blemish

steps.confusionAlert: Only the last line, 'מום קבוע הוי לשחוט עליו', is רבי יוחנן's own words. Everything before it is the משנה that he is commenting on.

phrases.english: And that which we learned in a mishnah:
A ewe that gave birth to a goat of sorts
and a goat that gave birth to a ewe of sorts
is exempt from the firstborn obligation,
and if it has some of the [mother's] features
it is obligated.
[Rabbi Yoḥanan:] It is a permanent blemish,
so one may slaughter it because of it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second statement by the same אמורא, added to the first.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A בכור that looks like a different species but has some of its mother's features has a מום קבוע and may be slaughtered.

steps.title: The first ruling clearly teaches something new
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא agrees that the first ruling (מום קל) teaches something new: it follows רב הונא and rejects רב חסדא and רבא.
steps.simpleTranslation: It makes sense that רבי יוחנן said 'even a slight blemish.' He is teaching us that he agrees with רב הונא, and he is rejecting the view of רב חסדא and רבא.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up a question. First it grants that the first statement is needed, so that it can then ask about the second one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'בשלמא' pattern means: 'This part I understand, but...' The first ruling picks a side in a real dispute. It sides with רב הונא, who said even the ear is enough, against רב חסדא and רבא, who required a bigger share. So it clearly teaches something.

keyTerms.meaning: Granted / it makes sense (sets up a contrast)

phrases.english: Granted, [the statement about] a slight blemish
teaches us [that the law is] like Rav Huna,
and to exclude [the view] of Rav Ḥisda and Rava.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins evaluating whether each of רבי יוחנן's two rulings is necessary.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether each of רבי יוחנן's statements adds a new teaching.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The first statement does add something: it sides with רב הונא against רב חסדא and רבא.

steps.title: What does the permanent-blemish ruling add?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the second ruling. A משנה already teaches that an animal whose mouth looks like a pig's has a מום, so why did רבי יוחנן need to say this?
steps.simpleTranslation: But the ruling about a permanent blemish, what does it teach us? That once the animal looks different, that counts as a blemish? We already learned that in a משנה: if its mouth looks like a pig's, that is a blemish!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why רבי יוחנן's second ruling was needed. It points to a משנה that already seems to say the same thing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The idea behind רבי יוחנן's ruling seems to be: 'an animal that looks different from its kind is blemished.' The משנה in פרק מומין (40a) already counts a lamb with a pig-like mouth as blemished. So רבי יוחנן's statement looks unnecessary.

keyTerms.meaning: It became different / changed in appearance
We already learned it [in a משנה]

phrases.english: But [the statement about] a permanent blemish
what does it teach us?
That since it looks different, it counts as a blemish?
We [already] learned it:
'And if its mouth is like that of a pig'
'that is a blemish!'

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא מוּם קָבוּעַ מַאי קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the 'בשלמא... אלא' structure by attacking the second ruling.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוחנן's statement that a mixed-looking בכור has a מום קבוע.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The statement seems unnecessary, because the משנה about a pig-like mouth already teaches that looking different is a מום.

steps.title: A suggested difference: pig versus goat
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests a way to defend רבי יוחנן. A pig is a species with no בכורה, but a goat is a species that does have בכורה, so maybe looking like a goat should not count as a מום.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you would say: there, the animal changed to look like something whose species has no בכורה holiness. Here, it changed to look like something whose species does have בכורה holiness.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא proposes a possible answer: the pig case and the goat case are different. This is a setup that the גמרא will reject in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Looking like a pig, a non-holy and non-kosher animal, is clearly a defect. Looking like a goat, which is itself a בכורה species, might not count as a defect. If so, רבי יוחנן would be teaching something new: even this kind of change is a מום.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you would say (introduces a suggested answer)

phrases.english: And if you would say,
there, it was changed into something
whose species has no firstborn sanctity,
[while] here, it was changed into something
whose species has firstborn sanctity,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a possible distinction to answer the קשיא of step 4.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since looking like a pig is already a known מום, רבי יוחנן's ruling seemed to add nothing.
steps.terutzMaskana: Changing into the look of a species that has בכורה holiness might not seem like a מום, so רבי יוחנן would be adding that it is one.

steps.title: That too was already taught: one big eye, one small
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the suggested difference. A משנה already teaches that one large eye and one small eye is a מום, even though that is a change within the animal's own holy species.
steps.simpleTranslation: This too we already learned in a משנה: if one of its eyes is large and the other is small, that is a blemish.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא knocks down the suggested answer. Another משנה already covers a change that stays within the animal's own holy species, and still calls it a מום.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An animal with uneven eyes has not turned into a non-holy creature. It simply looks strange within its own species. Since that already counts as a מום, the difference of 'holy species versus non-holy species' does not help. רבי יוחנן's ruling still seems to need a reason to exist.

keyTerms.meaning: This too we have already learned

steps.whatToRemember: The גמרא accepts רבי יוחנן's first ruling (מום קל). It finds his second ruling (מום קבוע for a mixed-looking בכור) hard to explain, since both the pig-mouth משנה and the uneven-eyes משנה already seem to cover it. Step 8 answers this.

phrases.english: This too we learned:
'One of its eyes is large'
'and one is small' [is a blemish].

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the distinction offered in step 5 and renews the קשיא of step 4.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proposed difference between changing into a holy species and changing into a non-holy species.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The uneven-eyes משנה already shows that a change within the animal's own holy species counts as a מום.

steps.title: A calf-sized eye seems to prove that any change counts as a מום
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא explains that 'large' means like a calf's eye. A calf has בכורה, so the only reason left seems to be that any change from a normal sheep is a מום. That would make רבי יוחנן's ruling unnecessary.
steps.simpleTranslation: A תנא taught: 'large' means as large as a calf's eye, and 'small' means as small as a goose's eye. The small eye is easy to explain, because a goose's species has no בכורה. But a calf's species does have בכורה! So isn't the reason that once the animal has changed, it counts as a מום?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to strengthen the point from Step 6: a change in appearance makes an animal blemished even when it looks like a species that has בכורה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 5 had tried to say that looking like a species with בכורה (a goat) is not a מום. Here a calf, which also has בכורה, still counts as a מום when the eye looks like its eye. So the rule seems to be 'any change is a מום,' and רבי יוחנן's ruling about a goat-like lamb would add nothing new.

keyTerms.meaning: A teacher of the משנה period; here, a ברייתא explaining the משנה
'It is understandable': this part fits, but the next part is a problem

phrases.english: And a tanna taught: 'large' means as large as that of a calf,
phrases.notes: This is explaining the משנה's case of one large eye and one small eye.

phrases.english: and 'small' means as small as that of a goose.
It is understandable for an eye as small as a goose's,
since there is no firstborn holiness in its species,
phrases.notes: Here 'its' means a bird, which has no בכורה at all, just like the pig case.

phrases.english: but an eye as large as a calf's —
its species does have firstborn holiness!
Rather, is it not because we say:
since it has changed, it is a blemish?
phrases.notes: If true, רבי יוחנן's ruling is not needed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a ברייתא to strengthen Step 6's rejection of the goat/pig difference.
steps.raayaObject: Any change in appearance is a מום, even toward a species with בכורה, so רבי יוחנן's ruling teaches nothing new.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא defining the large eye as a calf's eye and the small eye as a goose's eye.

steps.title: No — the large eye is a מום because it is a שרוע
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof. A calf-sized eye is a מום for a different reason: the animal has an oversized limb (שרוע), which the Torah lists as a מום.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. It is a מום because the animal is a שרוע (has a limb that is too big).
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the proof from Step 7 by giving a different reason for the calf-sized eye.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The large eye is not a מום because the animal 'changed.' It is a מום because one body part is too big, and the Torah lists שרוע by name (ויקרא כב:כג). So the ברייתא does not prove that every change is a מום, and room remains for רבי יוחנן to teach something new.

keyTerms.meaning: An animal with one limb larger than normal; a Torah-listed מום

steps.confusionAlert: The question is not whether the large eye is a מום. Everyone agrees it is. The only question is why: because of 'change,' or because of שרוע.

phrases.english: No, it is because it is a 'sarua' (an animal with an oversized limb).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof of Step 7 by giving another reason for the ruling.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the claim that the ברייתא proves 'any change is a מום.'
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The calf-sized eye can be explained by the separate Torah category of שרוע.

steps.title: Support from the משנה about blemishes found only in a person
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says the שרוע reason makes sense. It cites a משנה: all animal blemishes also disqualify a כהן, and a person has extra blemishes, such as both eyes large or both eyes small.
steps.simpleTranslation: This makes sense, as we learned in a משנה: these blemishes, whether permanent or passing, disqualify a כהן. A person has more blemishes than these: if both his eyes are large, or both are small.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a proof that the large eye is a מום because of שרוע. It starts by quoting a משנה; the next steps explain what we learn from it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה lists 'both eyes large' and 'both eyes small' as blemishes that apply only to a person. This means that for an animal, two equally large or equally small eyes is not a מום. That fact is the base of the proof.

keyTerms.meaning: So too it stands to reason: introduces support
A person has more (blemishes) beyond these

phrases.english: This too stands to reason, as we learned:

phrases.aramaic: מוּמִין אֵלּוּ, בֵּין קְבוּעִין בֵּין עוֹבְרִין — פּוֹסְלִין.
phrases.english: These blemishes, whether permanent or temporary, disqualify (a priest).
A person has more than these:
his eyes, both large, or both small.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts bringing support for the שרוע explanation of Step 8.
steps.raayaObject: The one-large-one-small eye is a מום because of שרוע, not because of change.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה about blemishes that apply to a person and not to an animal.

steps.title: Why two equal odd-sized eyes is a מום only for a person
steps.stepSummary: The extra rule for a person comes from the פסוק 'איש איש מזרע אהרן,' which requires a כהן to look like other כהנים. An animal has no such rule, so two big or two small eyes is not a מום for it.
steps.simpleTranslation: For a person it is written: 'איש איש מזרע אהרן' (any man from the offspring of אהרן), meaning we need a man who looks like the rest of אהרן's offspring. But for an animal, both eyes large or both eyes small is not a מום.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the source of the person-only rule. This sets up the final argument in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A כהן must look ordinary compared to other כהנים, so any unusual look disqualifies him. An animal has no such rule. So for an animal, simply looking different (two big eyes) is not a מום.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Any man from the offspring of Aaron' (ויקרא כב:ד)
Equal to (looking like) his fellow offspring

phrases.english: It is regarding a person that it is written:
'Any man from the offspring of Aaron,'

phrases.aramaic: דְּבָעֵינַן אִישׁ שָׁוֶה בְּזַרְעוֹ שֶׁל אַהֲרֹן,
phrases.english: so we require a man who is like the rest of Aaron's offspring,

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל בְּהֵמָה, שְׁתֵּיהֶן גְּדוֹלוֹת שְׁתֵּיהֶן קְטַנּוֹת —
phrases.english: but an animal with both eyes large or both eyes small —
that is not a blemish.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the key inference from the משנה quoted in Step 9.
steps.raayaObject: For an animal, a simple change in eye size is not a מום.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The פסוק 'איש איש מזרע אהרן' limits the 'looks different' rule to כהנים.

steps.title: So the one-big-one-small eye must be a שרוע
steps.stepSummary: If 'change' made an animal blemished, two big or two small eyes would also be a מום, and they are not. So one big and one small eye must be a מום because of שרוע.
steps.simpleTranslation: So if one eye is large and one is small, what is the reason it is a מום? If it is because of change, then two large or two small eyes should also be a מום! Rather, isn't it because the animal is a שרוע?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes its proof that the eye case is about שרוע, not about change.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two big eyes is also a change, yet for an animal it is not a מום. So 'change' cannot be the reason for the one-big-one-small case. The only reason left is that one eye is out of proportion, which makes the animal a שרוע. This backs up Step 8: the eye משנה is about שרוע, not change, so רבי יוחנן's ruling (a change into a species that has בכורה is a מום) does teach something new.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, is it not: introduces the only remaining explanation

steps.whatToRemember: This proof claims that one big and one small eye must be a מום because of שרוע, since two big or two small eyes are not a מום for an animal. Steps 12–13 reject this proof and show that the reason could still be שינוי.
steps.whyThisMatters: If this proof held, it would firmly rescue רבי יוחנן from the challenge of Steps 6–7. Steps 12–13 reject the proof itself, but the answer of Step 8 (שרוע) remains a possible way to defend him.

phrases.aramaic: אַחַת גְּדוֹלָה וְאַחַת קְטַנָּה, מַאי טַעְמָא?
phrases.english: One large and one small, what is the reason?
If it is because of change —

phrases.aramaic: אֲפִילּוּ שְׁתֵּיהֶן גְּדוֹלוֹת, שְׁתֵּיהֶן קְטַנּוֹת נָמֵי!
phrases.english: then even both large or both small should also be a blemish!
phrases.notes: But Step 10 showed they are not.

phrases.english: Rather, is it not because it is a 'sarua'?

steps.triggerLanguage: אַחַת גְּדוֹלָה וְאַחַת קְטַנָּה, מַאי טַעְמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses Step 10's inference to complete the proof of Step 8.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The proof argues that the one-large-one-small eye is a מום because of שרוע, not because of change. Steps 12–13 reject this proof.

steps.title: The גמרא rejects the proof: the reason could still be change
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes back on Step 11 and says the reason could really be שינוי, since a change from the normal form is a מום.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. Really, I can tell you the reason is change, and a change counts as a blemish.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the conclusion of Step 11, which said the reason must be שרוע. It returns to the idea that שינוי (change) is itself a מום.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 11 argued that 'change' cannot be the reason, because then two big eyes or two small eyes would also be a מום. Here the גמרא says the 'change' reason still stands. It still owes us an answer to that difficulty, and the next step gives it.

keyTerms.meaning: Really / actually (I hold my original position)
A change, a difference from the normal form

phrases.english: No, actually I will say to you
it is because of the change,
and a change counts as a blemish.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects Step 11's conclusion and brings back the 'change' reason.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the claim that the only explanation is שרוע.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Step 11 assumed that two big or two small eyes would also count as a change. The next step shows they do not.

steps.title: Why two big or two small eyes are not a real change
steps.stepSummary: Two big eyes can come from strong health, and two small eyes can come from weakness. One big and one small eye cannot be explained that way, so only that is a real שינוי.
steps.simpleTranslation: And about your difficulty, that even two big eyes or two small eyes should then be a blemish: there it is different. If the big eye came from extra health, both eyes should have been healthy and big. If the small eye came from extra weakness, both eyes should have been weak and small.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the difficulty from Step 11. Equal eyes, whether both big or both small, have a natural explanation, so they are not a change.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A very healthy animal naturally has big eyes, and a very weak animal naturally has small eyes. So when both eyes match, the animal is normal for its condition. When the eyes do not match, neither health nor weakness explains it, because those would affect both eyes equally. That mismatch is a true שינוי, and therefore a מום.

keyTerms.meaning: And as for what is difficult for you (formula that brings back an objection in order to answer it)

steps.whatToRemember: The supporting proof for שרוע fails. One big eye plus one small eye could be a מום simply as an unexplained שינוי, while two matching eyes are explained by health or weakness, so for an animal they are not a מום. The גמרא only shows that the 'change' reason is still possible. It does not rule out the שרוע answer of Step 8.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix this up with a כהן. For a כהן, two big or two small eyes IS a מום, because of 'איש איש מזרע אהרן' (Step 10). Here we are only talking about animals.

phrases.english: And as for what is difficult for you:
that even when both are large,
or both are small, it should be a blemish?
There it is different. If the big eye were because of extra health,
both eyes should have been healthy;
if the small eye were because of extra weakness,
both eyes should have been weak.
phrases.notes: So only mismatched eyes are a true change.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the defense begun in Step 12 by answering the objection from Step 11.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinction: a natural, explainable difference versus an unexplained mismatch.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: If change is a מום, any unusual eye size, even two matching big or small eyes, should be a מום.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only a mismatch that health or weakness cannot explain is a שינוי. One big and one small eye is a מום because of change, without needing שרוע.

steps.title: רבא tells a convert she need not worry about firstborn status
steps.stepSummary: A גיורת raised animals together with her non-Jewish brothers. רבא ruled that nobody follows רבי יהודה, who says a partnership with a גוי is obligated in בכורה.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was a certain convert whose brothers would give her animals to fatten. She came before רבא. He said to her: Nobody is concerned for this view of רבי יהודה, who said a partnership with a gentile is obligated in firstborn status.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic: a real case about animals owned together with a גוי. רבא rules that such animals are not obligated in בכורה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה brought a disagreement. רבי יהודה says an animal owned partly by a גוי still has בכורה, and the חכמים say it is exempt. Her brothers were גוים, so they were partners in the animals. רבא rules like the חכמים: the firstborn of these animals is not a בכור.

keyTerms.meaning: To fatten them (raising animals and sharing the profit)
There is no one who is concerned for it (this view is not followed)

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the practical halacha: an animal partly owned by a גוי is exempt from בכורה. The next story depends on this rule.

phrases.english: There was a certain female convert
whose brothers would hand over to her
animals to fatten.
She came before Rava.
He said to her: There is no one who is concerned
for this view of Rabbi Yehuda, who said:
a partnership with a gentile is obligated in firstborn status.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic, going back to the משנה's dispute about partnership with a גוי.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The halacha does not follow רבי יהודה. An animal partly owned by a גוי is exempt from בכורה.

steps.title: רב מרי בר רחל transfers the ears to a גוי, and his animals die
steps.stepSummary: רב מרי בר רחל gave a גוי ownership of the ears of his firstborn animals so they would not be בכורות. Still, he did not shear them or work them, and he gave them to the כהנים. His animals died out.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב מרי בר רחל had a certain flock. He would transfer ownership of their ears to a גוי. Still, he forbade shearing them and working with them, and he gave them to the כהנים. And the animals of רב מרי בר רחל died out.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a second story about partnership with a גוי. A rabbi used the rule from Step 14 to remove בכורה status, and something bad happened to him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because partnership with a גוי exempts an animal from בכורה, selling even the ears to a גוי removes its holiness. Yet רב מרי still treated the animals like בכורות: no shearing, no work, and he gave them to כהנים. The story ends with his flock dying, which suggests he did something wrong. The next steps explain what.

keyTerms.meaning: Shearing and work, both forbidden with a בכור

phrases.english: Rav Mari bar Rachel
had a certain flock of animals.
He would transfer ownership of their ears to a gentile,
phrases.notes: He means the ears of firstborn animals still unborn, so a גוי would be a partner and the animal would be exempt.

phrases.english: yet he forbade them for shearing and work,
and he gave them to the kohanim.

phrases.aramaic: וּכְלַאי חֵיוָתָא דְּרַב מָרִי בַּר רָחֵל.
phrases.english: And the animals of Rav Mari bar Rachel died out.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב מָרִי בַּר רָחֵל הַוְיָא לֵיהּ הָהִיא חֵיוָתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second story built on the same rule: partnership with a גוי exempts from בכורה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Selling part of a firstborn to a גוי removes its בכורה status, but doing so led to punishment.

steps.title: Why sell the ears if he treated them as firstborns anyway?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: if רב מרי kept all the rules of a בכור anyway, why did he bother selling the ears to a גוי?
steps.simpleTranslation: But since he forbade shearing and work and gave them to the כהנים anyway, why did he transfer ownership of their ears to a גוי?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges his behavior, which seems to contradict itself. He took away their holiness, but then acted as if they were holy.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the goal of selling the ears was to keep the animals for himself, it makes no sense to then give them to כהנים. He gained nothing, so what was the point of selling?

phrases.english: But since he forbade them
for shearing and work,
and gave them to the kohanim,
why did he transfer ownership of their ears to a gentile?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי מֵאַחַר דְּאָסַר לְהוּ בְּגִיזָה וַעֲבוֹדָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions what רב מרי did in the story of Step 15.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב מרי's choice to sell the ears to a גוי.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: He kept all the בכור rules anyway, so removing their holiness seems pointless.

steps.title: He wanted to keep the kohanim from sinning
steps.stepSummary: He sold the ears so the כהנים would not sin by shearing or working a holy בכור.
steps.simpleTranslation: Lest they come to a mishap with them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that he meant well. He wanted to protect the כהנים from a תקלה (a stumbling into sin).
steps.deeperAnalysis: A כהן who receives a real בכור might shear it or work it, and that is forbidden. Once the animal is not truly a בכור, such a mistake is no sin. So רב מרי gave the כהנים the animals as a gift without the risk.

phrases.english: Lest the kohanim come to a mishap with them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 16.
steps.terutzMaskana: It protected the כהנים from accidentally violating the holiness of a בכור.

steps.title: If his intent was good, why was he punished?
steps.stepSummary: If רב מרי acted to protect the כהנים, why did his animals die?
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, what is the reason the animals of רב מרי died out?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer in Step 17. A good motive should not bring a punishment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The story implies his flock died as a punishment. But Step 17 made his actions sound proper and even caring. So the גמרא asks what he did wrong.

phrases.english: If so,

phrases.aramaic: מַאי טַעְמָא כְּלוֹ חֵיוָתָא דְּרַב מָרִי?
phrases.english: what is the reason the animals of Rav Mari died out?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי הָכִי, מַאי טַעְמָא כְּלוֹ חֵיוָתָא דְּרַב מָרִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of Step 17 using the ending of the story in Step 15.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in Step 17 that he acted with good intent.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A good intention should not lead to a punishment like losing his flock.

steps.title: He was punished for removing their holiness
steps.stepSummary: Even with a good reason, he removed קדושה that the Torah had given the animals, and for that he was punished.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because he removed their sanctity.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that his sin was taking away the בכור holiness, even though he meant well.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Selling the ears was allowed on a technical level. Still, deliberately stopping the animals from becoming holy is improper. Good intentions toward the כהנים did not excuse undoing קדושה.
steps.whatToRemember: An animal partly owned by a גוי is exempt from בכורה, as רבא ruled. But deliberately using this to remove a בכור's holiness is frowned upon, even for a good reason. That is why רב מרי בר רחל was punished.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows the difference between what is technically allowed and what is proper: a legal loophole can still be wrong if it cancels קדושה.

phrases.english: Because he removed them from their sanctity.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 18 and closes the story.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Identifies the wrongdoing: a good motive does not cancel the wrong act.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: His good intention should have protected him from punishment.
steps.terutzMaskana: Removing קדושה from a בכור is wrong, even when done for a good reason.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: You should not cancel a בכור's holiness on purpose, even through a legal method and for a good reason.

steps.title: But רב יהודה allows blemishing a firstborn before birth
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the idea that removing a בכור's holiness deserves punishment. רב יהודה rules that a person may blemish a בכור before it is born.
steps.simpleTranslation: But didn't רב יהודה say: a person is allowed to put a blemish on a בכור before it comes out into the air of the world!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the answer it just gave in step 19. It brings a ruling from רב יהודה that seems to allow removing a בכור's holiness.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 19 said רב מרי was punished for removing holiness from his animals. But רב יהודה permits blemishing a fetus so that it is born unfit for the מזבח, which also removes holiness ahead of time. If that is allowed, why was רב מרי punished?

keyTerms.meaning: But didn't [so-and-so] say! (opens a challenge from another ruling)
To put a blemish on an animal
The air of the world, meaning being born
An אמורא whose ruling is quoted here

steps.confusionAlert: רב יהודה only permits the blemish BEFORE birth. Once the בכור is born, its holiness is fully in place, and blemishing it is forbidden.

phrases.english: But didn't Rav Yehuda say:
It is permitted for a person to put a blemish on a firstborn
Before it comes out into the air of the world!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer in step 19 that removing holiness deserves punishment.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in step 19 that רב מרי was punished for removing the animals' holiness.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רב יהודה permits removing holiness before birth by blemishing the fetus. So removing holiness before birth should not be a sin.

steps.title: A blemish removes only altar holiness, but the sale removed the priest's holiness too
steps.stepSummary: A blemish only takes away the animal's fitness for the מזבח, and it still goes to the כהן. רב מרי's sale took away even the כהן's rights.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, he removes it only from the holiness of the מזבח. He does not remove it from the holiness of the כהן. Here, he removes it even from the holiness of the כהן.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by showing that the two cases are different.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A בכור has two layers of holiness: it is fit for the מזבח, and it belongs to the כהן. A blemish removes only the first layer, so the כהן still gets the animal. Selling the ears to a גוי made the animal not a בכור at all, so it removed the כהן's layer too, and that went too far.

keyTerms.meaning: Altar holiness: the animal's fitness to be brought as a קרבן
Priest holiness: the כהן's right to receive the animal
There / here (used to contrast two cases)

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that a בכור's holiness has two separate parts. Avoiding one part can be allowed, while wiping out both is not.

phrases.aramaic: הָתָם מִקְּדוּשַּׁת מִזְבֵּחַ קָא מַפְקַע לֵיהּ,
phrases.english: There, he removes it from the holiness of the altar,
But he does not remove it from the holiness of the priest.

phrases.aramaic: הָכָא אֲפִילּוּ מִקְּדוּשַּׁת כֹּהֵן קָא מַפְקַע לֵיהּ.
phrases.english: Here, he removes it even from the holiness of the priest.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָתָם מִקְּדוּשַּׁת מִזְבֵּחַ קָא מַפְקַע לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 20.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the cases (חילוק): two different levels of holiness.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Blemishing a fetus and selling its ears both remove holiness in the same way, so both should be allowed.
steps.terutzMaskana: A blemish removes only the altar holiness. The sale to a גוי removes the כהן's holiness too, and that deserves punishment.

steps.title: Second reason: others might copy רב מרי without a proper sale
steps.stepSummary: Another explanation for the punishment: רב מרי knew how to make a complete sale. Others who saw him might copy him with an incomplete sale and end up misusing a real בכור.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you want, say: רב מרי בר רחל knew how to transfer ownership with a complete sale. But another person sees him, goes and does the same, and thinks it is the same thing רב מרי did. Through this he comes to a mishap.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a different answer to the question in step 18 about why רב מרי's animals died.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this answer, removing holiness is not the problem. The problem is that people could misunderstand what they saw. Someone might copy רב מרי with a weak, invalid sale and then shear or work an animal that is still a real בכור. רב מרי was punished for creating this risk.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you want, say (introduces an alternative answer)
A mishap or stumbling into sin

steps.whatToRemember: There are two reasons why רב מרי was punished: (1) he removed even the כהן's holiness from the animals; (2) others might copy him without a proper sale and come to sin with a real בכור.
steps.confusionAlert: This answer does not say that רב מרי's own sale was invalid. His sale worked. The danger was only to other people who would copy him the wrong way.

phrases.english: And if you want, say:
Rav Mari bar Rachel knew
How to transfer ownership with a complete sale,
But another person sees him,
And goes and does it himself,
phrases.notes: Without making a proper, complete sale.

phrases.aramaic: וְסָבַר רַב מָרִי מִילְּתָא הוּא דַּעֲבַד,
phrases.english: And thinks: this is the same thing Rav Mari did,
And through it he comes to a mishap.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second, independent answer to the question in step 18. This answer is not affected by the challenge from רב יהודה.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Alternative explanation: concern that others will misunderstand and make mistakes.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב מרי was punished for removing holiness that the Torah gave.
steps.terutzMaskana: He was punished because others watching him could copy him with an invalid sale and come to sin.

steps.title: משנה: כהנים and לוים are exempt, by a קל וחומר
steps.stepSummary: A new משנה rules that כהנים and לוים are exempt from the laws of a firstborn donkey. This is learned through a קל וחומר from what happened in the מדבר.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: כהנים and לוים are exempt, through a קל וחומר. If they exempted the firstborn of ישראל in the מדבר, it makes sense that they exempt their own.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא's discussion of רב מרי is over, and a new משנה begins. It teaches who is exempt from פטר חמור.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the מדבר, the לוים took the place of the firstborn of ישראל, and the לוים' animals took the place of ישראל's firstborn animals. So the לוים 'freed' the firstborn of others. If they could free other people's firstborn, they should certainly free their own.

keyTerms.meaning: Our משנה (marks the start of a new משנה)
An argument from a lighter case to a stronger one
A firstborn donkey, which must be redeemed with a lamb

steps.whyThisMatters: This opens the next topic: who is obligated in the laws of a firstborn. The גמרא will now examine this קל וחומר.

phrases.english: Mishnah:
Priests and Levites are exempt,
phrases.notes: Exempt from redeeming a firstborn donkey.

phrases.english: From a kal vachomer:

phrases.aramaic: אִם פָּטְרוּ אֶת שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל בַּמִּדְבָּר,
phrases.english: If they exempted those of the Israelites in the wilderness,
phrases.notes: The לוים and their animals replaced ישראל's firstborn (במדבר ג:מה).

phrases.aramaic: דִּין הוּא שֶׁיִּפְטְרוּ אֶת שֶׁל עַצְמָן.
phrases.english: It is only logical that they should exempt their own.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה after the story of רב מרי is finished.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: כהנים and לוים are exempt from the laws of פטר חמור, because a קל וחומר from the מדבר shows it.
